https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgl.text: Image source, World Central Kitchen Image caption, Seven World Central Kitchen humanitarian workers were killed in Israeli strikes in April 2024 By Tinshui Yeung Published 8 hours ago The UK, Canada and Australia have described as "shameful" Israel's decision not to launch a criminal investigation into strikes on a World Central Kitchen (WCK) convoy in Gaza in 2024, which killed seven humanitarian workers. The victims were three British nationals, a Pole, an Australian, a Canadian and a dual US-Canadian citizen. A joint statement by the three foreign ministries said: "The victims of this incident and their families deserve justice and accountability, and we will continue to seek answers on their behalf." Earlier, Israel's ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, defended the decision, saying "there was no criminal intention" and therefore "no criminal responsibility". The statement said that on 1 April 2024, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) fired on the WCK convoy as it was delivering food to civilians in Gaza. "In the more than two years since, we have been pressing for Israel to swiftly and thoroughly consider the case and hold those responsible to account," it said. The three countries said the fact that Israel's announcement came on World Humanitarian Day, "while the world honoured the courage and sacrifice of humanitarians, was particularly egregious". It also said the WCK attack was only "one of countless incidents in Gaza where there has been no accountability", as Gaza remains "the deadliest place to deliver aid", with 186 humanitarian workers killed in 2025. It urged Israel to comply with its obligations under international humanitarian law and do more to ensure that humanitarian staff can carry out their work safely. Who were the World Central Kitchen workers killed in Gaza? 'Serious failures' In its statement on Wednesday, the IDF said the presence of an armed guard with the convoy had not been flagged to it before the convoy set off, and that he was falsely identified as a Hamas fighter. It also accused the convoy of deviating from the route co-ordinated with the military. Notwithstanding "serious failures" in the process that led to the killings, "the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct," the IDF said. Prior to the statement by the three countries, Australia summoned Hillel Newman . Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong said her country was "outraged" by the Israeli government's decision. She also said there were still many "unanswered questions" about the strikes, including why, if the first strike on the convoy was "a catastrophic error", two further strikes followed just minutes apart. Poland's foreign ministry also said on Thursday that it was "very disappointed" and had summoned Israel's ambassador in Warsaw. The founder of World Central Kitchen, Jose Andres, described the decision as "wrong" and "painful for all of us", demanding an independent commission to investigate. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has not publicly responded to the latest statement from the UK, Australia and Canada, but he previously said that the military had "unintentionally" killed the volunteers. The statement came after a harsh exchange of words between UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar over Israel's plans to open tenders for the construction of about 1,200 settlement homes in a strategically important part of the occupied West Bank. Israeli settlements are illegal under international law and plans to build in the so-called E1 area - east of Jerusalem - have long been internationally condemned. Miliband condemned the publication of the tender as "an unacceptable and destructive act", and called on Israel to "halt E1 plans immediately, retract the tender and stop all settlement expansion". In response, Saar said on social media that he rejected "outright" Miliband's statement. "The Jewish people have the right to live throughout the Land of Israel, just as the British have the right to live in London and throughout the United Kingdom," he wrote. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, File photo of the Israeli settlement of Maale Adumim in the occupied West Bank next to the so-called E1 project in East Jerusalem, taken in February 2026 While the IDF had decided not to launch a criminal investigation into the strikes on the WCK convoy, it announced in the same statement that it would carry out a criminal investigation into the killing by Israeli forces of five-year-old Palestinian girl Hind Rajab and six of her relatives in Gaza in 2024. It also said it would similarly investigate the killing of 15 Palestinians , including medics and a UN worker, in March 2025. Their bodies were found buried in shallow graves a week later next to crushed vehicles. https://telex.hu/foto/2026/08/22/magyar-.text: Menü Kereső Dráma a föld alatt: képek a hazai barlangi mentés kemény pillanataiból Fotó Szépkilátás Gyakorlat a bükki Szepesi-barlangban, ahol egy 2009-es gerincsérüléses baleset mentését már több alkalommal újrajátszotta és modellezte a mentőszolgálat, ezért ilyen terepen, mint a Szepesi-barlang százméternyi aknasora, még gyorsabban, kíméletesebben hajtja végre a mentést – Fotó: Kovács Márton Ostyáni János Tenczer Gábor Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Barlangász, barlangi mentő és fotóriporter, aki 15 éve fotózza társait és a mentőszolgálat munkáját – Kovács Márton igyekszik a maga módján láthatóvá tenni mindazt, ami egy-egy mentés vagy gyakorlat során a föld alatt történik. A fotósnak Mentők lámpafényben címmel februárban nyílt kiállítása a Magyar Természettudományi Múzeumban, amit a nagy sikerre tekintettel meghosszabbítottak decemberig. Cikkünkben a kiállítás anyagából válogattunk. Kovács Márton a kilencvenes évektől fogva barlangászik, húsz éve barlangi mentőként is, mellette fotóriporterként ügynökségeknek, hírügynökségnek fotózik. Mint elmondta, a barlangászat neki nem sport, és nem is csak a barlangokról szól. Számára ugyanannyira, ha nem még fontosabb a barlangász közösség, a barlangász szubkultúra, ami harminc éve körülveszi. „Most, hogy már nem tartozom a leggyorsabb, legügyesebb, legerősebb barlangászok második vonalába sem, sok energiát fordítok arra, hogy a közösségen belül a nem technikai örökségünket, old school barlangász attitűdjeinket tovább tudjuk örökíteni a következő generációk értékrendjébe is” – mondta. A 2023-as törökországi mentésen a Morca-barlangban a hazai háttércsapat tagja volt. Mint felidézte: a mentéssel kapcsolatban ellátott feladatai közül nem arra a legbüszkébb, hogy sikerült leakasztania a katonáktól a magyar Air Force One-t; nem arra, hogy Budapestről sikerült vasárnap éjjel kinyittatnia egy török vérbankot, hogy vigyenek fel helikopterrel vért a sérültnek a barlanghoz; nem is arra, hogy a mentés utánra intézett másfél nap tengerparti szállodát a srácoknak; hanem arra, hogy sikerült megszervezni azt, hogy a hordágy felszínre érkezésére érkezzen meg egy helyi vadász egy csomagtartónyi sörrel és borral a magyar csapathoz. A Magyar Barlangi Mentőszolgálat (BMSz) idén ünnepli megalakulásának 65. évfordulóját. Működése során közel 600 olyan mentőakciója volt, ahol barlangászok, túrázók vagy siklóernyős pilóták annyira nehezen megközelíthető helyen kerültek bajba, és ahol más mentőszervezetek nem nagyon tudtak volna érdemben segíteni. A BMSz nem csak barlangi mentést végez, deklarált célja, hogy segítséget tudjon nyújtani a felszínen is, a nehezen megközelíthető helyeken bajba került túrázóknak, sérülteknek. Mentettek már elhagyott bányába esett kutyát, lichthofba szorult varjút, vettek már le holttestet villanyoszlopról, és hoztak le rosszul lett darukezelőt a toronydaru fülkéjéből. Víz alatti mentés a jósvafői Kossuth-barlangban, ahol a mentést az Amphora Egyesület kutató búvárai végezték, a Barlangi Mentőszolgálat a logisztikai támogatást nyújtotta és előkészítette a barlangot a transzportra – Fotó: Kovács Márton A barlangi mentők könnyű terepnek azt a járatot hívják, ami legalább három ember szélességű, nincsenek nagy kövek, nem csúszik a talaj, ahogyan itt, a Solymári-ördöglyukban. A hordágynak oldalanként három füle van, ilyen terepen hat ember viszonylag kíméletesen tudja mozgatni a sérültet – Fotó: Kovács Márton A Szendvics nevű szűkület a Mátyás-hegyi-barlangban. Itt egy végtagsérüléses túrázót rövid időre elaltattak, majd a ficamodott végtag reponálása után hordágyon hozták felszínre a fájdalomcsillapító utóhatásai miatt – Fotó: Kovács Márton A polárból készült mentőhálózsákot, amely tökéletesen illeszkedik a hordágyba, a kihűlés ellen használják a mentők. A hazai barlangok átlagos hőmérséklete nagyjából 10 Celsius-fok, az emberi testé 37, ez a kettő abban a pillanatban elkezd kiegyenlítődni, amint nem mozgunk – Fotó: Kovács Márton Gyakorlat a Vass Imre-barlangban. Nincs ideális mentési létszám, a hazai barlangjainkban előforduló kisebb mentéseknél a 22-28 fős csapat elégséges szokott lenni, ha kisebb a létszám, akkor a párhuzamosan végezhető feladatokra nincs ember, viszont ha túl sokan vannak, akkor lassul a csapat, már egy nehezebb mászás, egy rövid kötéltag vagy egy szűkület is lelassíthatja a csoport mozgását – Fotó: Kovács Márton A mentéseknél szinte ugyanolyan eszközöket használnak, mint barlangászásnál, mert azokat jól ismeri mindenki, és bizonyítottan barlangállóak. Ferde húzásoknál egy flaschenzug elnevezésű csigasort használnak, ami megsokszorozza a húzóerőt – Fotó: Kovács Márton A sikeres mentésekhez sokak sokrétű és gazdag barlangász tapasztalatára van szükség, ehhez sok év barlangászás kell, hogy legyen az emberben. A BMSz szakmai vezetői pozícióiba olyanok kerülnek, akik organikusan váltak a közösség húzóembereivé, akiknek a tudását társaik is mind elismerik, és adnak a véleményükre – Fotó: Kovács Márton Ellensúlyos felhúzás az Abaligeti-barlang oldalágában. Ez a technika kíméli a sérültet a hordágyban, kíméli a hordágyat és a kikötési pontokat is, viszont nagy koncentrációt igényel, ugyanis a sérült és a mentő össze van kötve. A hordágy és az ellensúlyként viselkedő mentő mozgását külön kontrollálják – Fotó: Kovács Márton Hordágy mozgatása omladékon a Vass Imre-barlangban. Ilyen helyeken különösen körültekintőnek kell lenni, mert a hordágyat nem lehet csúsztatni, és az esésvonalban sem lehet mozogni a leguruló kövek miatt – Fotó: Kovács Márton Gyakorlat a Ferenc-hegyi-barlangban. A barlangi túravezetői végzettség megszerzésének korábban feltétele volt, hogy a hallgatóknak el kell menniük egy mentési gyakorlatra, és be kell szállniuk a feladatokba. A részt vevő megfigyelés segít megérteni a mentés folyamatait, nehézségeit, talán segít az óvatos és gondos túravezetői attitűdök kialakításában. Ilyen alkalmak után többen is jelentkeztek már a mentőszolgálathoz próbaidős tagnak – Kovács Márton Élő csiga a Solymári-ördöglyukban. Ideális esetben a felhúzásra használt kötél nem ér a falhoz, de bonyolult aknákban ez ritkán van így, ilyenkor terelni kell a kötelet. A leggyorsabb módja ennek az, ha a barlangi mentő a beülőjébe akasztja a csigát, és nyújtott lábaival eltartja a kötelet a faltól. Amint utoléri őt a hordágy, átvált a hordágy kísérőjének szerepébe, és igazítja, hogy ne akadjon el – Fotó: Kovács Márton Az abaligeti II. oldalágban az ember nagyon fiatal, szűk járatokban halad, amik hol laposak, keskenyek, aktív patakosak, máskor híg agyaggal telítettek. Előfordult olyan gyakorlat, ahol 400 métert 8 óra alatt tett meg a hordágy, azt is úgy, hogy kétszer kivették a sérült szerepét vállaló barlangi mentőt – Fotó: Kovács Márton Az ideális barlangi mentő magasan képzett barlangász, rendelkezik az összes kötéltechnikai tanfolyam tudásanyagával, releváns barlangjáró tapasztalattal, és könnyen tud váltani az irányító és a végrehajtó szerepek között – Fotó: Kovács Márton Kedvenceink

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Milo Yiannopoulos speaking during a rally in the US in 2021. He has declared himself ‘firmly off the Trump train’. Photograph: Julio Cortez/AP View image in fullscreen Milo Yiannopoulos speaking during a rally in the US in 2021. He has declared himself ‘firmly off the Trump train’. Photograph: Julio Cortez/AP Far right (US) ‘GB News wouldn’t touch him’: Milo Yiannopoulos will struggle to fit in with UK right wing ‘Alt-right’ agitator and former Trump backer deported from US is said also to be too extreme for Reform Helena Horton Sun 30 Aug 2026 13.50 EDT Last modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 14.51 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google As he arrives back in the UK after being deported from the US by the Trump administration, the far-right provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos may be wondering what lies ahead for him in his native country. The “alt-right” agitator, 41, made his name in the US by promoting Donald Trump and associating with his allies before the 2016 election. But now the Trump administration has unceremoniously dumped the former Breitbart News editor back in the UK after he allegedly overstayed his visa. He has also made plenty of disparaging comments about the president, including that he is “firmly off the Trump train”. Those in the rightwing ecosystem in the UK say Yiannopoulos is now too extreme to find a prominent berth back home. The commentator started his career at the Daily Telegraph, where he wrote a controversial blog until 2011, when he started his own website, the Kernel. In 2014 he started working for the former Trump adviser Steve Bannon at Breitbart News, before moving to the US and promoting far-right causes. He left Breitbart after a controversy over a video in which he appeared to condone sexual relations with boys as young as 13. He later said “sloppy editing” and his “British sarcasm, provocation and gallows humour” had created the wrong impression and denied endorsing paedophilia. Since he left the UK, GB News has become the ascendant broadcast outlet of the right, but he is unlikely to find a place there. A source at the channel said: “We wouldn’t touch him with a barge pole, not in a million years. GBN had a few odd people to start with and we’ve got rid of them.” Yiannopoulos after his arrest by federal immigration agents in New Orleans. Photograph: Department of Homeland Security/Reuters Of the provocative positions that brought him notoriety in the US, the GB News source said: “He won’t make much money out of it here, he appeals entirely to an American audience. It’s a bigger country and you have a bigger pool of fruit loops.” There is a growing subsection of rightwing provocateurs in the UK who have been deemed too controversial for the main channels but have established niche brands of their own. The journalist Dan Wootton was suspended from GB News after a guest on his show made sexually inappropriate comments about a female journalist, and after leaving he now has his own channel. The former TalkTV host Mike Graham has also set up his own independent show. He was sacked after the company said he had failed to cooperate with an investigation into a racist post that appeared on one of his social media accounts. Graham said the racist comment had been the result of his account being hacked. It is understood that Reform UK will not accept him into its ranks. His former colleague at Breitbart, Raheem Kassam, is close to the party’s leader, Nigel Farage, and is in the UK for Reform’s national conference. Kassam, who is British but now lives in the US, claimed he was kept updated on the deportation of Yiannopoulos, who he accused of making “lurid and false accusations” against him. He added: “I got word last month that he was about to be deported. On Thursday night, I got a call. As overly dramatic as it may seem. ‘We got him. In Louisiana.’” The Maga influencer Laura Loomer has claimed to have reported Yiannopoulos to immigration enforcement over his expired visa. View image in fullscreen Laura Loomer (front, centre) celebrates with Yiannopoulos at a congressional primary election night event in West Palm Beach, Florida, in August 2020. Photograph: Allen Eyestone/AP One political party that may accept Yiannopoulos is Restore Britain , which is led by Rupert Lowe, a former Reform MP who had a falling-out with Farage. Restore has accepted a number of characters viewed as too extreme for Reform, including the convicted criminal Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, also known as Tommy Robinson. Yiannopoulos has praised Lowe, calling him “fantastic” and urging those on the UK hard-right to join Restore. He said “the rising generation of young British activists” all “support Restore” and has taunted Reform’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, online, telling him “you’re gonna lose all your votes to Rupert”. The Guardian contacted Lowe to ask whether he would accept Yiannopoulos as a party member or adviser but did not receive a response. Kassam said: “He’s certain to resurface in Britain shortly. Perhaps as an adviser to Rupert Lowe, or perhaps as a contestant on some third-tier reality TV show.” Yiannopoulos used to have more political influence; he was offered a speaking slot at the Conservative Political Action Conference, or CPAC, in 2017 after he had been supportive of Donald Trump during his run for his first presidency. He was deported to the UK on Friday, according to US authorities. A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said Yiannopoulos “legally entered the country” in May 2019 through New York City but then “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”. In 2022, Yiannopoulos worked on Kanye West’s short-lived 2024 White House campaign, and his social media account suggests he was working one of the rapper’s companies. Last year, Yiannopoulos said he was “never going back home” because the UK needed a “mass deportation programme”. Yiannopoulos was approached for comment. Storm Austen batters France and UK with winds of up to 160 km/h Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 23/10/2026 - 15:46 GMT+2 Huge waves, uprooted trees and damaged boats mark Storm Austen's arrival in France and the UK. Gusts of up to 160 km/h have battered Brittany, while fallen branches have blocked roads in southern England. … More Storm Austen , the first named storm of the 2026 autumn season, battered coastal areas of France and the UK on Friday 23 October, bringing powerful winds, heavy rain and towering waves . Brittany, Cornwall and Devon were among the hardest-hit regions, with gusts reaching 160 km/h at Pointe du Raz in Finistère, while winds of up to 80 mph were forecast for exposed headlands in south-west England. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Along the Finistère coast, gusts of 120 to 140 km/h whipped up rough seas. At Lanildut harbour, waves several metres high crashed against a navigation marker, yachts rocked violently at their moorings and a pleasure boat was left capsized and partially submerged . Heavy rain flooded parts of the harbour , while fallen branches littered nearby roads. Further along the coast, large waves pounded the shoreline at Le Conquet, where boats remained moored in the port. In Rennes, emergency crews used chainsaws to remove a large tree uprooted beside the River Vilaine, temporarily blocking traffic on a nearby boulevard. Across the Channel, fallen branches forced the closure of a road in Hayle, Cornwall, as workers cleared the debris. Strong winds and downpours also swept across southern England, with Devon among the areas exposed to the worst conditions. The storm's strongest winds and heaviest seas were concentrated along the Atlantic and Channel coasts before the weather system moved eastwards across northern France and southern England. https://www.israelnationalnews.com/news/.text: I chose not to publish anything on October 7th, that day belongs to the victims. Any argument about what the world has done since risked becoming another voice in the noise, another demand upon a day for remembrance. For the families slaughtered in their homes, the young people hunted at a music festival, the hostages dragged into Gaza. Those murdered in the attempted genocide against the Jewish people, and everyone whose life was shattered. Their names, their faces, the lives they should have lived. For one day, I wanted to leave the space to them. There is plenty I could write now. About those who chose the anniversary of the greatest massacre of Jews since the Holocaust to march against the only Jewish state. About the targeting of Jewish organisations, the poison on campuses, the public figures whose statements somehow struggle to let murdered Jews remain the subject of their own remembrance. The equivocation, the appropriation, the people for whom even our grief must first pass a political test. But they have taken enough. Enough of our attention, enough of our energy, enough of the space in which we should be able to live, remember, celebrate and simply be Jewish. This week, I want to give that space to people who deserve it. Students dancing through a university campus with a Torah above their heads. A captain and passengers whose courage prevented catastrophe. A son turning his father’s love of Jewish music into a source of communal pride. European Jews opening synagogue doors and welcoming a Torah into a community preparing for its future. Across different countries, different generations and radically different circumstances, something familiar is happening. We are carrying our story forward. This article is dedicated to those who refuse to let anybody else decide where it ends. Kol Hakavod to the Jewish students of Leeds University. On Simchat Torah, Jewish students at Leeds sang, danced and celebrated publicly around their university campus, a Sefer Torah held above their heads. Young Jews, in Britain, carrying their inheritance through the place where they are building their futures. Simchat Torah marks the completion of the annual reading of the Torah and the beginning of the cycle again. We reach the end, then return to the beginning. We lift the scrolls, we sing, we dance. We are a people carrying its story in its arms. Three years ago, in Israel, that festival was torn apart by slaughter. A morning that should have belonged to celebration became a morning of murdered families, burning homes and desperate calls for help. Music became inseparable from the images of young people running for their lives. That is part of what those students carry now, too. They belong to a generation whose Jewish adulthood is being shaped by October 7th and everything that followed. They have seen how quickly a campus can become a place where Jewish identity invites interrogation, where belonging comes with conditions and where other people presume the right to decide which parts of yourself you should conceal. Yet still, they danced, with the Torah above their heads, their voices raised, their Jewishness unmistakable and this belongs to a wider story. Hillel International describes students responding to campus hostility by turning towards Jewish community, coming for Shabbat dinners and staying to build friendships and take on leadership. Its Jewish learning programmes reach thousands of students each year; this autumn, it is supporting expanded Shabbat experiences at more than 130 campus Hillels across the world. Young Jews are gathering, learning, taking their places around Friday-night tables. Discovering, or rediscovering, what it means to belong to this people. There is something deeply powerful about that choice. When the world makes your identity feel like a liability, you reach for the people who understand its value. You learn more about the inheritance others demand you disown, you find a community, then help make it stronger. Hatred has consequences, but sometimes, the young Jew they hoped to intimidate becomes the young Jew organising the next Shabbat dinner. Sometimes, the identity they hoped to weaken becomes the source of a person’s strength. Sometimes, our children lift a Torah above their heads and dance. How many generations prayed that their descendants might do that freely? How many parents and grandparents carried those same words through places where being Jewish could cost them everything? There they were, on a British university campus, our children, our future. Kudos to the Jewish students of Leeds University, and to young Jews everywhere choosing to gather, learn and celebrate. You are giving the rest of us reasons to stand a little taller. Kol Hakavod to Captain Smit Machchhar and the passengers and crew of Flight FlyDubai 1073. I have not written since the attempted hijacking of flydubai Flight 1073, and I will not let the moment pass without recognising those whose bravery helped save everyone aboard. Captain Smit Machchhar was attacked inside his cockpit on the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv. Badly wounded, he fought back and managed to unlock the cockpit door. Israeli passengers overpowered the attacker; a passenger helped steady the aircraft before two off-duty pilots took over and landed it safely. There are moments when the distance between life and death becomes unimaginably small. A movement, a decision, a few seconds in which somebody finds the strength to do something that the rest of us can barely comprehend from the safety of our chairs. Captain Machchhar found that strength and when the door opened, others found theirs. Suddenly confronted with the possibility that somebody intends to kill you and everyone around you, there is no time to prepare yourself for that knowledge. Yet passengers moved towards the danger, towards the wounded captain, towards the place where their intervention could make the difference. Strangers became responsible for one another. I will not name the attacker here. I want us to remember Smit Machchhar, I want us to remember the passengers who confronted the attacker, the crew who helped and the pilots who brought the aircraft down safely. An Indian captain and Israeli passengers, people with different backgrounds and different lives, brought together while on an ordinary journey and confronted with an extraordinary demand. They met it. We know what it means to take responsibility for one another when survival demands action and only because these people acted, families could be reunited, people could go home, lives could continue beyond that flight. Ordinary things, made extraordinary by how close they came to being lost. Kudos to Captain Smit Machchhar, to the passengers and crew who helped save Flight 1073, and to everyone aboard carrying its memory. May you find healing, comfort and peace, and may our gratitude reach you. Kol Hakavod to Hilton Nathanson and Bishnat . After his father died in 2021, Hilton Nathanson established Bishnat to pass on the Jewish pride his father had given him, bringing people together through Jewish music. Then, in the weeks after October 7th, he found that arranging a Jewish concert in Britain had become difficult. A son wanted to honour his father through the music he loved. To fill a room with people, share something beautiful and send them home feeling closer to one another and somehow, in this country, that became difficult. Hilton’s answer has been to keep bringing people together. Bishnat’s next concert, Be The Light, takes place in London on October 13th, with the hope that people will leave more confident in their Jewish identity and more willing to stand up for it. There is something that happens when we sing together which no statement of solidarity can quite reproduce. You recognise a melody that belonged to your childhood, perhaps to a parent or grandparent who is no longer here. You hear the people around you singing it too, you watch your children discover it for themselves. For a moment, the distance between generations closes. The people who gave us those songs are present in the way we sing them. The people who will carry them after us are learning their place in the story. That matters particularly now, when so much of Jewish communal life is consumed by responding to what is done to us. The next incident, the next slur, the next institution that needs reminding of its responsibilities. We need places where our identity fills the room on its own terms. Where our children can see that being Jewish is a source of warmth, laughter, friendship and pride. Where the friends who stand beside us can share in the life they are helping us defend. We cannot allow the entirety of our children’s Jewish inheritance to become an explanation of why other people hate them. Give them the songs, the joy, the experience of a room full of people who love being who they are. Hilton has built something that makes those moments possible. A father’s love of music, carried forward by his son, becoming a gift to people that father never met. There is a beautiful Jewish continuity in that. Kudos to Hilton Nathanson and Bishnat. May every child in that room hear something they will one day want to pass on. Kol Hakavod to the Jewish communities rebuilding in Budapest and Leipzig. In Budapest, the historic Rákospalota synagogue has returned to Jewish worship. Built a century ago, it served its community for only eighteen years before the Holocaust devastated that community. For decades afterwards, the building was used to store books and newspapers for Hungary’s national library. Now, restored and rededicated, it is once again a place of Jewish prayer. A building made for Jewish voices, reduced to storage, but then those voices return. There is something about that which reaches far beyond architecture. The restoration of a synagogue carries a decision about the future, that there will be people here to pray, people here to gather, people here to teach their children what this place means. The history stays with them, it must. The murdered cannot be restored, the generations that should have filled those rooms cannot be recovered. No ceremony, however moving, can repair that loss, but Jewish life can return. While in Leipzig, Germany, a small Jewish learning and prayer group has received its first Torah scroll in community history. Fifteen members, meeting in private homes, now have a scroll on a ninety-nine-year loan from a congregation in Maryland, with its public dedication having taken place this week. Fifteen people, ninety-nine years, look at the confidence contained within those two numbers. A community small enough to gather in somebody’s home, making provision for Jewish life almost a century into the future. That is endurance with its sleeves rolled up. Somebody searching for a Torah, somebody answering the appeal, people across an ocean helping Jews in Germany build something that will outlast them. The continent where Jewish communities were devastated by the Holocaust is still home to Jews who are restoring, learning, praying and preparing for the generations to come. There is no innocence in that hope. These communities know the history of the places in which they live, they know the challenges of the present and they build anyway. In Budapest, a synagogue returns to its purpose. In Leipzig, a small community receives the Torah through which it will carry its story forward. We should honour the people who make that happen: the rabbis, donors, volunteers and community members whose work turns the language of Jewish continuity into something you can walk into, hold and hear. Kudos to the Jews of Budapest and Leipzig, and to those rebuilding Jewish life across Europe. May your communities grow, your doors remain open and your children know the strength of what you have renewed. Four stories. Leeds, Flight 1073, music as a sense of pride, Budapest and Leipzig. A Torah raised above young heads, a wounded captain opening a door, passengers acting to save lives, a son carrying his father’s music forward, a synagogue reclaimed, a small community making plans for ninety-nine years. Look at what these people are giving us. Courage we can recognise, pride we can share, places to gather, reasons to believe in the generations ahead. I kept October 7th for remembrance and that remembrance stays with me today. The families in their homes, the young people at the festival, those dragged into captivity. The people we knew, and those we came to know only through the terrible fact of their murder. Every one of them had a life beyond the way it was taken. People they loved, songs they knew, things that made them laugh, plans for the following week, the following year. Futures. We owe them the dignity of remembering all of that and we owe the generations who come after them a Jewish life they can embrace with pride. So thank the captain, honour the passengers, stand beside the students, fill the concert, support the communities opening their doors. Let our children see us doing it. Let them inherit the songs as well as the stories, the joy as well as the grief, the courage as well as the knowledge of what courage has cost. Those who tried to end the Jewish story left us graves and ghosts, we remember every one, but they dd not get to write the final chapter. Our children are already writing the next.
